d101.text: Last time, we compared the frog and the mosquito. In both, the young look nothing like the adult, but the frog has three stages, and the mosquito has four. Then Basil asked a tricky question!

d201a.text: A little honeybee is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

d201b.text: Look for a fuzzy, striped body!

d201c.text: Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

d401.text: Round one. Which came first? One, the egg. Two, the chicken. Three, neither: it goes round and round. Show me with your fingers.

d403.text: One, the egg! The egg is always the first word when we say the stages.

d404.text: Three. Every egg came from a hen, and every hen came from an egg. It just goes round.

d405.text: Three! A loop goes round and round, so nothing comes first.

d601.text: Be an egg! Shrink down. Quietly.

d602.text: You are an egg, warm under the mother hen. Days go by. Crack! You hatch. You are a fluffy chick.

d603.text: You eat, and you grow, and your feathers grow. Weeks go by. You are an adult hen.

d604.text: One morning, you lay an egg of your own. It hatches into a chick, and round it goes again.

d605.text: So where did it start? You joined in at the egg, but you could have joined anywhere.

d406.text: The answer is three: neither! Three fingers? One finger up!

d701.text: Look closer. Put your finger anywhere on the loop, and follow the arrows round. You always come back.

d702m.text: It is like day and night! Which comes first? Neither. They just keep going round.

d703.text: The stages in a life cycle are repeated. So there is no first or last stage.

d704p.text: Repeated means it happens again and again. So we never put numbers on the stages, because none of them is first!

d706.text: The stages in a life cycle are repeated. There is no first or last stage.

d801.text: Showdown! Double points. Momo's homework has one mistake. Line one, two, or three? Show me with your fingers.

d802m.text: One: in both, the young do not look like the adult. Two: the mosquito larva lives near the water surface, but the beetle larva lives on land. Three: the mosquito has four stages, but the beetle has three.

d804b.text: Three! The mealworm turns into a pupa before it becomes a beetle. So the beetle has four stages too!

d806.text: Three fingers? Put up two more on your score hand!

d901m.text: Oops! The beetle's pupa lies so still that I forgot to count it. So how are they different?

d902.text: Look closer. The stages are the same, so now we compare their physical features.

d904b.text: Physical features are the parts we can see. The wriggler is thin, and hangs at the water surface. The mealworm is golden and hard, and crawls on land!

d906.text: Observable characteristics include the number of stages and the physical features of the animals.

d1001.text: Why do life cycles matter? Look! The butterfly from last time is laying an egg on the lime plant.

d1003.text: Life cycles ensure that living things of the same kind can continue to live on Earth.

d1006m.text: With too few lime plants, there would be fewer larvae, fewer pupae and fewer butterflies. So we plant more, and the cycle keeps going!

c1003.text: Same or different? Compare them both! Count the stages! Three or four! Round and round! No first, no last!

d1201.text: Show me your score hand! More than one? You beat the Buddies. Three fingers? High five!

d1202.text: Did you spot the honeybee? It was on a flower of the lime plant!

d1203p.text: Here is a fun fact! A queen honeybee can lay more than a thousand eggs in a single day. That keeps the bees' life cycle going!

d1301.text: Next time: a magnet, a steel pin and a copper wire! The pin and the wire are both metal. Which one will the magnet pull? One, the steel pin. Two, the copper wire. Three, both. Lock in your answer!

h860.text: Let's read today's key words together! Ready?
